---
title: "curse of dimensionality"
---

## samples, features & dimensions

- samples are rows: individual observations, such as patients.
- features are columns: measurements describing each observation.
- dimensions are feature axes; a dataset with $n$ samples and $d$ features has shape $(n,d)$.
- high-dimensional data has many features; this is different from simply having many samples.

## why more dimensions can be difficult

- **sparsity:** maintaining a fixed resolution requires rapidly more data. ten bins per axis create $10^d$ cells: ten in one dimension, but ten billion in ten dimensions.
- **distance concentration:** with many similarly scaled, weakly dependent features, nearest and farthest distances can become less distinct. this depends on the data distribution and distance metric.
- **boundary concentration:** for points uniformly distributed in a unit ball, the fraction within the outer 10% of its radius is $1-0.9^d$: about 65% at $d=10$ and 99.997% at $d=100$.

## why it matters

- knn, k-means, and dbscan can struggle when distances no longer distinguish useful neighbours or clusters.
- irrelevant features can obscure signal, increase computation, and encourage overfitting when samples are limited.
- linear models, kernel methods, and neural networks are not automatically immune; assumptions, regularisation, and sample size still matter.

## what helps

- remove irrelevant or redundant features using [feature selection](../training-evaluation/feature-engineering.qmd#feature-selection-extraction).
- consider [dimensionality reduction](../dimensionality-reduction/index.qmd) while checking that useful structure is retained.
- regularise supervised models and evaluate choices on held-out data.
- fit learned transformations within training folds to avoid leakage.
